final_message:
Plant Something, Anything

There is a notion abroad that gardening is for people who own land, and leisure, and a certain sort of hat. I hold that this is a slander, got up by those who have never been pleased by a radish.

Consider the case. You put a seed into the ground, which is a very small act, and about as much trouble as losing a button. You then go away and do other things. When you come back, which you will do a great many times more often than is needed, something has happened. A small green hook has pushed up out of the dirt, and is looking about it with the air of a person who has just arrived at a party and does not know the host. You will feel, I promise, an absurd pride. You did nothing, and you take all the credit. This is the whole secret of the pleasure, and it is a harmless one.

I know the objections. You have no garden. Neither had Diogenes, and he got on very well with a tub. A window-sill will hold a pot of basil; a pot of basil will hold your attention longer than most things on a screen. If you have no window-sill, you have a friend who has, and friends are always glad to be asked about their tomatoes. Nobody has ever been asked this question and been sorry.

Then there is the matter of the lessons. A garden teaches patience, they say, and humility, and the cycle of the seasons. It does teach these; but it teaches them in a sly way, by killing your first lettuce. You learn that the world does not hurry on your account. You learn that the slug is a creature of fixed principles. You learn, towards August, that a single zucchini plant is capable of a generosity that borders on menace, and that your neighbors have begun to lock their doors.

But these are the small returns. The large one is this: that for a few minutes in the day, with your hands in the soil and the sun on your neck, you are not thinking of the news, or the office, or what was said at the meeting. You are thinking of whether the beans want water. It is a cheap and honest sort of peace, and it is sold at the hardware store for about three dollars a packet.

So go and buy the packet. Plant it in a coffee can if you must. Then wait, and be surprised.
